General-purpose optimisation with heuristic and derivative-free methods

Source: R/calibrar-main.R
optimh.Rd

optimh() provides a unified interface to the heuristic and derivative-free optimisation methods available through calibrar. It is intended for objective functions that are expensive, noisy, non-smooth, stochastic, or otherwise difficult to handle with standard gradient-based optimisers.

Usage

optimh(
  par,
  fn,
  gr = NULL,
  ...,
  method = c("AHR-ES", "Nelder-Mead", "SANN", "hjn", "bobyqa", "CMA-ES", "genSA", "DE",
    "soma", "genoud", "PSO", "hybridPSO", "mads", "hjk", "hjkb", "nmk", "nmkb"),
  lower = -Inf,
  upper = +Inf,
  active = NULL,
  control = list(),
  hessian = FALSE,
  parallel = FALSE
)

Arguments

par

A numeric vector or list. The length of par defines the number of parameters to be estimated (i.e., the dimension of the problem).

fn

The objective function to be minimised. It should accept a parameter vector (or list, depending on the wrapper) as first argument and return either a scalar value (single-objective) or a numeric vector (multi-objective).

gr

Function computing the gradient of fn. It is included for API consistency with optim2() and calibrate(), but is ignored by most methods available through optimh().

...

Additional arguments passed to fn and gr.

method

Optimisation method to use. Available choices are "AHR-ES", "Nelder-Mead", "SANN", "hjn", "bobyqa", "CMA-ES", "genSA", "DE", "soma", "genoud", "PSO", "hybridPSO", "mads", "hjk", "hjkb", "nmk", and "nmkb".

lower

Lower bounds for parameters. One value or a vector of the same length as par. NA is treated as -Inf. Default is unconstrained.

upper

Upper bounds for parameters. One value or a vector of the same length as par. NA is treated as Inf. Default is unconstrained.

active

Boolean vector of the same length as par, indicating if the parameter is used in the optimisation (TRUE) or held at a fixed value (FALSE).

control

A list of control options. Common options include ncores, run, master, verbose, REPORT, restart.file, gradient, and gr.method. Additional solver-specific options may be passed through to the underlying optimiser.

hessian

Logical. Should a numerically differentiated Hessian matrix be returned? Currently not implemented.

parallel

Logical. Enable parallel computation (e.g., for replicated evaluations and/or numerical gradients) using up to control$ncores cores.

Value

A list in the same general format as optim2(), typically including:

par

The best parameter values found.

value

The value of fn at par.

counts

Number of function and gradient evaluations reported by the underlying solver, when available.

convergence

Convergence code returned by the underlying solver.

message

Additional information returned by the optimiser, if any.

hessian

A Hessian estimate when supported and requested; otherwise usually NULL.

Details

optimh() uses the same interface conventions as optim2() and calibrate(): parameters may be supplied as a vector or list, box constraints can be enforced through lower and upper, and subsets of parameters can be held fixed through active.

The available methods include both genuinely heuristic/global algorithms (for example "AHR-ES", "CMA-ES", "DE", "genSA", "PSO") and a few derivative-free local searches (for example "Nelder-Mead", "bobyqa", "hjn", "nmk"). The function name should therefore be read broadly: it is the package entry point for optimisation methods that are typically useful when classical smooth, gradient-based optimisation is not the best fit.

Analytic gradients are accepted for interface consistency, but many methods implemented through optimh() ignore gr. Likewise, not all methods return Hessian information even when hessian = TRUE is requested.

Choosing a method

Heuristic and evolutionary methods are often useful for rugged, multi-modal, or stochastic objective functions. Derivative-free local methods may be a better first choice when the objective is deterministic but gradients are unavailable or unreliable. Method choice should still reflect the structure of the problem: locality versus global exploration, box constraints, stochasticity, and computational cost.

See also

optim2(), calibrate(), ahres(), gradient()

Other optimisers: ahres(), calibrate(), optim2()

Author

Ricardo Oliveros-Ramos

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
optimh(
  par = rep(0.5, 5),
  fn = sphereN,
  lower = -5,
  upper = 5,
  method = "AHR-ES",
  control = list(maxit = 200)
)
} # }
